title: Dorchester County finding solutions to Eagle Creek flooding - NewsBreak
text: SUMMERVILLE, S.C. (WCBD) – A flood-prone area in the Lowcountry is getting special attention after repeat flooding has the community looking for answers. Dorchester County is deciding on next steps to lower the water levels at Eagle Creek. After more than a year of research, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) says they’ve found a cost-effective way to mitigate flooding in the area. LeShawn Watson says she lost her Dorchester County house to a fire and had another severely damaged from hurricane Irma. “It leaves you with a sense of PTSD because once you’ve experienced one, you’re just waiting for it to happen again,” Watson said. “I don’t feel like I’m in control and am able to help the situation. I try to get out of the house and move stuff to higher ground.” The county and USACE opened a discussion with residents Wednesday about their plan for the flooding. “A very viable project for construction that has a very good and positive benefit to the ecosystem because of the adjacent wetlands that will be benefitted from it,” USACE project manager Mark Messersmith said. “Also a pretty good reduction of water surface elevations for the neighborhoods around there.” The project would remove more than 11,000 cubic yards of soil, giving water room to spread out. This is something they say will reduce the water level and allow more water flow through the creek. Through a year and a half of research, the corps weighed multiple options. Everything from building flood walls, to raising house and building elevations. Through their studies, they found upstream benching to be most effective. “Taking the side slope of a creek and cutting into that to allow more natural infiltration of water,” Messersmith said. “It’s considered a nature-based solution for flood risk management projects. That allows connection back to the flood plain and the wetlands that are adjacent to, that have been cut off historically from that berm that was built up on the outside edge of that creek.” Watson says she just wants action for the safety of her family and home. USACE is refunding the county the surplus funds from their research. However, the county says they are still exploring ways to raise funds for the rest of the project, which could cost around $500,000.
